previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with metastatic breast cancer and recent PFO closure was admitted for evaluation of transient left facial droop noticed by her husband the prior evening. She denied symptoms and had no persistent deficits on exam, though initial testing showed subtle left-sided motor slowing. MRI revealed no acute infarct but showed linear enhancement in the left frontal operculum, concerning for either a small subacute stroke or metastatic involvement. Given her risk factors—including high cholesterol, recent PFO closure, and malignancy—a transient ischemic attack (TIA) was diagnosed. Her symptoms resolved completely during the hospital stay. Dual antiplatelet therapy was continued, but statin therapy was withheld due to advanced cancer. She was discharged home with stroke education, instructions to follow up with cardiology, and a rolling walker for support.

consulted who recommended possible trial of tigan. She was 
discharged with new medication of reglan TID with meals.    

She was readmitted ___ - ___ after with similar symptoms. 
She became acutely hypoxic without a clear trigger, and after 
transfer to ICU was found to have ASD. PFO closure was performed 
on ___, and ASA and Plavix were started. On ___, after she was 
discharged from the hospital following her PFO closure, a left 
facial droop was noticed by her husband. She had no other 
symptoms at that time. Given her risk factors, she was admitted 
to the hospital for further work-up. Her neurological exam was 
initially notable for left upper motor neuron arm weakness and 
slow finger tapping without evidence of facial droop. Symptoms
resolved, and MRI showed no stroke, likely TIA.  
 
She again developed a flare of nausea with dry heaves and 
epigastric abdominal pain. She presented to the ED on ___, and 
was treated with morphine (initially for her pain), Ativan and  
home medications. She improved and tolerated PO, so was sent 
home with follow up with Dr. ___ ongoing treatment with 
botox
injections for her severe gastroparesis. 

However, that evening she again developed recurrent nausea and 
dry heaves with associated abdominal pain. Emesis is non-bloody 
and primarily phlegm. Pain is mid epigastric, constant, and 
doesn't radiate. She also has chronic back pain, up to ___ at 
its worst, but currently stable. No fevers or chills. No
dysphagia or odynophagia. No CP, SOB or cough. No palpitations. 
Last BM last night was normal and she does report flatus. No 
other complaints.

invasion. There was no lymphovascular invasion. Both hormone

prior
lower axillary dissection. Her Oncotype recurrence score was 20.
This corresponds to a 13% ___ risk of recurrence assuming
___ years of tamoxifen. We would expect somewhat better results
for management of lobular carcinoma with an aromatase inhibitor.
On the other hand, this was apparently recurrent disease after
prior radiation therapy, which might have diminished tumor
sensitivity to additional therapy.  

Adjuvant treatment was discussed, both endocrine therapy and
chemo-endocrine therapy. She favored endocrine therapy alone
strongly and this was felt to be an acceptable choice.

presented to the ED on ___ with nausea, vomiting, and

Her CT abdomen/pelvis returned consistent with numerous hepatic
and osseous metastases. In the hospital, she underwent a liver
biopsy which revealed a carcinoma compatible with a breast
primary tumor. Estrogen receptor was positive. HER-2/neu was not
assessed.
